The company has said it uses biometric data — facial recognition, fingerprints, or similar — to track when employees arrive and leave. Under California's rule, that kind of processing triggers the risk-assessment requirement in § 7150, and § 7152(a)(6) requires the assessment to identify the safeguards that address the risk. In Spain, the data protection authority (AEPD) fined Cartonajes Bañeres €220,000 for photographing employees' faces at an entry-point device without telling them the images would be used that way, and without a completed risk assessment for the biometric processing. Where biometric data is used for time-and-attendance or access-control monitoring, the assessment has to address whether that specific use is necessary and proportionate compared with less-intrusive alternatives — not just note that a badge-in system exists. This is a foreign decision under different law, cited only by analogy, and the aid translation above has not been checked against the full 200-page decision; whether it applies here depends on this company's own facts about its biometric processing and how it was disclosed. (Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (Spanish Data Protection Agency), Cartonajes Bañeres, S.A., decision PS-00361-2023, 5 January 2024; foreign supervisory-authority decision, cited by analogy.)
